sections.COMMENTS: ï»¿This seismogenic source was first proposed by Calamita et al. (1992) based on geological and geomorphological evidence. Following the 24 August 2016, Mw 6.0, Amatrice earthquake a 10-20 cm-high coseismic break formed along the Mt. Vettore primary bedrock fault scarp. The breaks were interpreted by several investigators as evidence for primary slip along the underlying seismogenic fault. Other workers used InSAR evidence to contend that the scarp was the result of settling of the loose deposits lying on the steep western slope of Mt. Vettore. On 30 October the Mw 6.5, Norcia earthquake caused the same phenomena observed two months earlier, but the scarp reached a maximum height of about 2 meters. The debate on the nature of these ruptures is still ongoing. While many workers believe the 30 October ruptures to be an undisputable proof of primary faulting, other workers contend that much of the observed deformation is related to gravitational collapse of the western flank of Mt. Vettore under the action of strong ground shaking, and that the remainder of the deformation may reflect slip on secondary faults branching off the main seismogenic fault at a depth of 1-3 km. This view is supported by the rather shallow dip of the main rupture plane (<45Â°) as revealed by focal mechanisms and InSAR data elaborations, making it mechanically unlikely for the main rupture plane to propagate up to the surface. Given these contrasting, views we believe the role of the Mt. Vettore fault as evidence of a primary seismogenic rupture still awaits clarifications and confirmation.
